# Documents

A document can display a 3D plot as a static figure or an interactive
viewer. This article uses knitr’s output switching, supplies accessible
descriptions and arranges plots on a page. Quarto’s R engine uses the
same chunk options. Installation is covered in [Get
started](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/ggplot3d.md); HTML
viewers also need [htmlwidgets](https://www.htmlwidgets.org/) and
[svglite](https://svglite.r-lib.org/), described in [Interactive
viewing](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/viewer.md).

## A static figure

The motor-car data record weight in thousands of pounds, fuel economy in
miles per US gallon and gross horsepower. Printing the plot uses its
chosen scene backend and the document’s graphics device. The default
backend draws vector geometry; this article’s SVG device keeps those
paths scalable.

``` r

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d() +
  labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg", z = "horsepower")
p
```

![Motor cars positioned by weight, fuel economy and horsepower, with
higher-power cars toward the upper part of the
box.](documents_files/figure-html/static-1.svg)

## HTML, PDF and Word

Set the chunk option `view3d = TRUE` to embed the interactive viewer in
HTML. The following chunk runs that switch. The figure dimensions are in
inches, and become widget dimensions at 96 pixels per inch. Facet
panels, titles, strips and legends follow the plot’s layout.

``` r

p
```

For PDF and Word output, that same option draws a static vector scene.
The document device determines the image format: a PDF device retains
vector geometry for a PDF document, and a PNG device samples it into
pixels for Word. With `view3d = FALSE`, the chunk uses the backend
configured on the plot.

Quarto accepts the equivalent option in its cell metadata. This is the
same plot object created above.

```` markdown

``` r
p
```
````

## Dense surfaces on a web page

An SVG figure stores each face of a surface as its own path, so a finely
meshed surface can weigh several megabytes in an HTML page. The chunk
option `raster3d` draws the data of such a plot into one embedded image
with `backend_3d("hybrid", rasterise = "all")`, described in [Output
backends](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/backends.md);
axes, panes, grid lines and text stay vector graphics, so a stylesheet
can still recolour them. `raster3d = TRUE` does this for every plot of
the chunk. A number is a file size in bytes: the chunk draws the vector
figure first, redraws it with the embedded image only when the file is
larger, and keeps the smaller of the two.

The image has the chunk’s `dpi` pixels per inch, which knitr multiplies
by `fig.retina` for HTML. The articles on this site use the setup below.
A 6.5 inch figure fills a 776 pixel column at about 120 pixels per inch,
and `fig.retina = 2` doubles that for high-density screens.

``` r

knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg", fig.width = 6.5,
  dpi = 120, raster3d = 1e5)
```

## Accessible descriptions

[`alt_text_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/alt_text_3d.md)
describes the layer types, mapped variables and initial camera angles.
The generated description supplies the default alternative text for
static figures and an accessible group name around HTML viewers. Inspect
it before adding words about what the figure communicates.

``` r

alt_text_3d(p)
#> [1] "3D plot. Layers: Point (x = wt, y = mpg, z = hp). Camera: azimuth -60 degrees, elevation 30 degrees, roll 0 degrees; orthographic projection."
```

An explicit chunk `fig.alt` takes precedence. A description supplied by
`labs(alt = ...)` takes precedence over the generated layer description.
The example below describes the relationship the reader can inspect in
the motor-car plot.

``` r

described <- p + labs(alt = paste(
  "Motor cars plotted by weight, fuel economy and horsepower.",
  "Heavier cars generally have lower fuel economy."))
alt_text_3d(described)
#> [1] "Motor cars plotted by weight, fuel economy and horsepower. Heavier cars generally have lower fuel economy."
```

When a chunk prints several plots, supply a vector of descriptions in
their printed order. Each static figure gets its own alternative text.

``` r

p
```

![Motor cars seen from azimuth minus sixty
degrees.](documents_files/figure-html/several-plots-1.svg)

``` r

p + coord_3d(azimuth = 30)
#> Coordinate system already present. Adding coord_3d() replaces it.
```

![The same motor cars seen from azimuth thirty
degrees.](documents_files/figure-html/several-plots-2.svg)

## Composing plots

[patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) arranges ggplot
objects. Each 3D scene compiles at the physical size of its panel, so
camera projection and mark sizes follow the final layout. Stack the plot
above a second view to give each one the document column’s width.

``` r

other <- p + coord_3d(azimuth = 30)
#> Coordinate system already present. Adding coord_3d() replaces it.
patchwork::wrap_plots(p, other, ncol = 1)
```

![Two motor-car plots stacked vertically with different camera
angles.](documents_files/figure-html/patchwork-1.svg)

[cowplot](https://wilkelab.org/cowplot/) also preserves the independent
scenes. Its composition below contains a 3D view and a 2D view of the
same cars. These arrangements are static figures; use a faceted ggplot
with the viewer for a live multi-panel document.

``` r

flat <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL["blue"], size = 3) + labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg")
cowplot::plot_grid(p, flat, ncol = 1)
```

![A 3D motor-car plot above a 2D scatterplot of weight and fuel
economy.](documents_files/figure-html/cowplot-1.svg)

[Combining 2D and 3D
graphics](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/combining-2d-3d.md)
shows shared scales and plots placed on planes inside a scene.

## Saving a raster figure

Choose the scene sampling resolution on the backend, then set the saved
image’s pixel dimensions through the device resolution. Both settings
use the intended physical size. The temporary file below is six inches
wide and four inches high at 144 dots per inch.

``` r

raster <- p + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 144))
#> Coordinate system already present. Adding coord_3d() replaces it.
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
ggsave(path, raster, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 144)
file.info(path)$size > 0
#> [1] TRUE
unlink(path)
```

[Output
backends](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/backends.md)
explains the rendering choices. [Exporting plots and
scenes](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/export.md) writes
model files and native SVG, TikZ or Asymptote output.
